Criterion: Verify that all safety supporting hardware elements (SSHEs) are safe. Standard: SPA SSHEs are identified. SSHE performance meets SPA processing requirements. SSHEs are of mature/proven technology with safety critical application heritage. SSHEs are designed to detect failures. These SSHEs may include but are not limited to the following: circuit cards, internal and external buses, signals/discretes, interfacing subsystems, feedback loops, cockpit/control station input/output (I/O), and Cross Channel Data Links, processors, FPGA, ASICs, backplanes, data storage devices, connectors, and power supplies. SSHEs are designed with reliable components and meet system reliability requirements. Method of Compliance: Verification methods include analysis, test, and inspection. Inspection verifies that the SSHEs of the SPA are identified/defined. Hazard analysis ensures hazards are traced to applicable SSHEs. Verify through analysis and/or test that SPA SSHEs and applicable components have the following performed as appropriate: a. Acceptable level of burn-in time completed without failure. b. Supplier acceptance testing (e.g., parts screening, sample lot acceptance testing). c. Failure Modes, Effects and Criticality Analysis (FMECA) performed. d. Electronic components supporting safety critical applications are tested to safety critical standards. e. FMET on hardware supporting SCFs. f. Qualification testing required for expected flight envelopes. Inspection and analysis ensure that all testing conducted at vendor and prime developer facilities adequately verifies hardware performance. References: JSSG-2008 Appendix A: 3.3.1, 3.4.1, and 3.4.5 cover components and parts pedigree; 3.1.11.11.2 addresses integrity of signal transmission MIL-HDBK-217: Reliability Predictions of Electronic Equipment MIL-STD-882: (see also MIL-STD-882D) DoD JSSSEH RTCA DO-254 RTCA DO-255 SAE ARP4761-1996 FAA AC 20-152 FAA TSO-C153: Appendix 1 section 4.f design assurance of hardware elements

versions.title_at_revision: Hardware element supporting safety-critical function(s) performance
versions.text: Standard: 1. Verify that all HESSs are safe. System processing architecture HESSs are identified. HESS performance meets processing requirements. Hardware elements supporting SCF(s) are of mature and proven technology with safety-critical application heritage. Hardware elements supporting SCF(s) are designed to detect failures. These HESSs may include but are not limited to the following: circuit cards, internal and external buses, signals, discretes, interfacing items, feedback loops, I/O, CCDLs, processors, field programmable gate arrays, application specific integrated circuits, backplanes, data storage devices, connectors, and power supplies. Hardware elements supporting SCF(s) are designed with reliable components and meet system reliability requirements. In addition, for designs utilizing MCP environments: 2. The processor family, model, and architectural and performance details (e.g., clock rate, total number of processing cores) of each MCP have been documented including known processor errata and deficiencies. Any known uses of the MCP in safety-critical applications have been documented to include known issues with its use in the given applications. Documented MCP errata, deficiencies, and issues have no adverse impact to the integrity of SCF operation or have been mitigated and shown to be safe. 3. The processing cores and other resources that are hardware enabled, and hardware disabled in the MCP are identified. Methods used for hardware disabling are identified. Hardware enabled processing cores and other resources that are functionally deactivated by MCP settings maintain the configured state throughout system operation. Mechanisms are in place to detect and accommodate inadvertent state changes to maintain the integrity of SCF operations. 4. For processing cores supporting SCFs, the lowest level cache is dedicated in its physical entirety to its respective processing core. Additionally, higher levels of cache are dedicated to processing cores either in their physical entirety or through use of a partitioning approach that allocates portions of cache to individual processing cores. Cache partitioning approaches do not unacceptably degrade SCF performance. 5. Data coherency is implemented, maintains the integrity (value and timing) of data associated with safety-critical processing across the MCP environment, and ensures the integrity of SCF operation. 6. Unused processing cores within an MCP are hardware disabled or functionally deactivated. Processing core activation and deactivation mechanisms ensure functionally deactivated processing cores remain functionally deactivated and functionally activated processing cores remain functionally activated. The MCP environment performs periodic monitoring during operation to ensure processing core activation and deactivation scheme does not change. Fault handling techniques maintain the integrity of SCF operation in the presence of changes in activation state (e.g., functionally deactivated processing core becomes functionally activated). 7. The failure modes of all processing cores, chip resources, and components of an MCP, whether hardware enabled, hardware disabled, functionally activated, or functionally deactivated, have been identified, are understood, and mitigations are in place to prevent adverse impacts to SCF operation in the event of their occurrence. 8. The MCP hardware contribution to the processing of SCFs is shown to be safe, deterministic, and in compliance with latency and performance requirements. 9. Interface management approaches, between processing cores and external to the MCP, are identified for each processing core to include rates, prioritization, routing, error management, interference resolution, and methods for ensuring consistency across shared memory. 10. Interference channels and areas of possible resource contention have been identified with their associated mitigations necessary to prevent adverse impacts to the integrity of SCF operation. Processing conditions that can increase the likelihood of interference or resource contention are identified. 11. Failure modes of the MCP have been identified along with their detectability. Critical failures have been identified and are detectable. Detectable failure modes are shown to be detected during PICFO and safely managed by the system. The system provides a safe response to MCP failure modes (single or combination) IAW fault tolerance requirements. 12. A safe approach is used for managing the features and settings of each processing core and resource in an MCP. All configurable features and settings of the MCP are identified and the flight configuration of the MCP settings are documented. The deactivation of processing cores and resources within an MCP through the use of features and settings does not adversely impact the integrity of SCF operation. Mechanization of MCP settings ensures settings remain persistent during operation. Fault conditions that can result in changes to the MCP settings are detectable and safely accommodated. All dynamically modifiable performance features of the MCP (e.g., dynamic modification of clock rates), to include all features that can impact deterministic processing, are identified and how each will be configured to eliminate or minimize processing changes in order to support SCF processing. Features of the MCP that have the potential to adversely impact the integrity of SCF operation (e.g., result in non-deterministic operation, create interference channels or resource contention that cannot be characterized) are disabled or safely mitigated to ensure no adverse impact to the integrity of SCF operation. 13. The MCP is designed to fully support an AMP or BMP scheme for processing cores processing a SESS. The MCP does not permit (by design or settings) the dynamic allocation of a process or VM to another processing core processing a SESS. Processing schemes used on processing cores not processing a SESS do not have any nominal or failure mode impacts to SESS processing. 14. Microcode update mechanisms are identified and a control plan established that prohibits unauthorized updates by controlling and authorizing updates only after thorough evaluation and test. Microcode update procedures are repeatable, consistent, and include methods for verifying the correctness of the installed update. Updates do not have a detrimental impact on SCF processing. 15. The MCP hardware interrupt configuration and design is identified. Multicore processor hardware interrupts are serviced in a safe and deterministic manner that does not impact other non-interrupted processing cores (and VMs as applicable) that are operating in the MCP environment. Interrupt routing and servicing schemes utilized provide for deterministic, stable SCF operations. Shared interrupts are not utilized for SCF operations (exception: a full MCP reset interrupt). Interrupts supporting a non-SCF process or processing task do not impact SCF processing. 16. The design, routing, and arbitration scheme of the processor interconnect and other resources used to interface processing cores and resources within the MCP ensure the integrity of SCF operation. The design and routing utilized do not introduce unacceptable latency or cause unacceptable jitter. Arbitration of messages support deterministic SCF operation compliant with latency and performance requirements. Failures in non-safety-critical processes or processing tasks do not adversely impact the ability of the processor interconnect or resources used for interfacing, their routing, or arbitration to support the integrity of SCF operations. Method of Compliance: Prior to entering flight test, verify the standard by the following method(s): The number next to an MoC line item corresponds to the numbered line item in the standard that is being verified: 1. Verification methods include analysis, test, and examination. Examination verifies that the HESSs of the SPA are identified and defined. Hazard analysis ensures hazards are traced to applicable HESSs. Verify through analysis and test that SPA HESSs and applicable components have the following performed as appropriate: a. Acceptable level of burn-in time completed without failure. b. Supplier acceptance testing (e.g., parts screening, sample lot acceptance testing). c. Failure modes, effects, and criticality analysis performed. d. Electronic components supporting safety-critical applications are tested to safety-critical standards. e. Failure modes and effects testing on hardware supporting SCFs. f. Qualification testing required for expected flight envelopes. Examination and analysis ensure that all testing conducted at vendor and prime developer facilities adequately verifies hardware performance. In addition, for designs utilizing MCP environments: 2. Analysis verifies that all MCP errata, deficiencies, and issues have been analyzed for safety impact, and have no adverse impacts to the integrity of SCF operation or have been safely mitigated. 3. Examination of MCP configuration documentation and settings verifies that processing cores that are hardware enabled and hardware disabled have been identified and confirms how processing cores will be hardware enabled or hardware disabled. Analysis and test verify that the mechanism to enable and disable processing cores maintains the configuration as set. Analysis and test verify that inadvertent changes to state are detected and safely accommodated to maintain the integrity of SCF operation. 4. Examination of MCP design and configuration documentation verifies that lowest level cache is dedicated in its entirety to its respective processing core. Examination verifies that higher levels of cache are dedicated to individual processing cores either in their physical entirety or through a partitioning approach. Analysis and test verify that the cache architecture and any partitioning scheme(s) utilized support the integrity of SCF operation. 5. Analysis and test verifies that the data coherency mechanization maintains the integrity (value and timing) of data used by SCFs and ensures the integrity of SCF operation. 6. Examination of MCP settings confirm how processing cores will be functionally activated or deactivated, and that unused processing cores are hardware disabled or functionally deactivated. Analysis and test verify that the mechanism to activate or deactivate the processing cores maintains the configuration as set. Testing verifies that the MCP environment periodically monitors the state of processing core activation or deactivation and detects any changes in the activation state. Testing verifies that fault-handling techniques maintain the integrity of SCF operation for failures that change the activation state. 7. Failure modes and effects analysis and FMECA document failure modes of the MCP and identify their potential impact to SCFs. Analysis, testing, and simulation of chip-level failures verifies that failure mitigations are in place to prevent adverse impacts to the integrity of SCF operation. Analysis, testing, and simulation of chip-level failures verifies that failures of processing cores, chip resources, and components not supporting SCFs do not adversely impact the integrity of SCF operations, or that their effects have been mitigated to prevent adverse impacts to the integrity of SCF operation. 8. Analysis and test verifies that the hardware provides deterministic operation and meets latency and performance requirements for SCF operation. 9. Analysis verifies that the interface management approaches utilized by the MCP (between processing cores and external to MCP) have been identified and provide adequate rates, priorities, routing, error management, interference resolution, and methods for ensuring consistency across shared memory supporting the integrity of SCF operation. Testing, including FMET, verifies that the functional operation and performance of the interface management approaches meet requirements and are adequate for SCF processing. 10. Analysis of the MCP hardware identifies all interference channels and areas of resource contention, processing conditions that can contribute to interference or resource contention, and associated mitigations. Testing verifies that the MCP responds as expected under conditions that can produce interference or resource contention and that mitigations employed are adequate to prevent adverse impacts to the integrity of SCF operation. The testing is performed over a comprehensive set of expected operating conditions including the known worst-case operating and timing conditions that can result in interference or resource contention. The testing covers all known interference channels, areas of possible resource contention, and associated mitigations. 11. Failure analysis (e.g., FMEA, FMECA) verifies the MCP failures have been identified, the detectability of each failure, and whether each failure is a critical failure. Analysis and testing, including FMET, verify the detection of failures and the system response supports fault tolerance requirements. 12. Examination of MCP design and configuration documentation verify that the following are identified: configurable features, dynamically modifiable performance features, and the defined configuration of the settings for all features. Analysis and test verify that the deactivation of processing cores and resources within an MCP through features and settings do not adversely impact the integrity of SCF operation. Analysis and test verify that the MCP settings mechanization scheme maintains the settings per the standard and that the settings utilized support deterministic, stable SCF processing and disable features that can influence deterministic operation (e.g., power saving features), cause interference channels, or resource contention. Analysis and testing show that unintended changes in settings are detected and safely accommodated. 13. Analysis and testing verify that the MCP supports an AMP or BMP scheme for processing cores processing a SESS and that other schemes utilized for processing cores not processing a SESS have no safety impact on SESS processing. The analysis also shows that the MCP will not dynamically allocate a process or VM to another processing core processing a SESS. 14. Examination of CM documentation and microcode update procedures verify that control plans and update procedures are in place for safely handling microcode updates, including fully evaluating the impact to SCF processing. Testing verifies that microcode updates can be performed repeatedly, consistently, and verify the installation is correct. Testing verifies that the microcode update does not adversely impact the integrity of SCF operation. 15. Examination of MCP design and interrupt configuration documentation verifies that the configuration approach for hardware interrupts has been identified. Analysis and test verify that the routing and servicing scheme facilitates deterministic, stable SCF operations; does not impact non-interrupted processing cores (and VMs as applicable); and that non-safety-critical interrupt handling does not impact safety-critical processing. 16. Examination of the MCP design documentation verifies that the design, routing, and arbitration schemes of the processor interconnect and other resources used for interfacing have been defined. Analysis and test verify that the design and routing employed do not introduce unacceptable latency or unacceptable jitter into messages supporting SCF operations. Analysis and test also verify that the arbitration scheme utilized prioritizes those messages supporting safety-critical processing to ensure compliance with latency and performance requirements and that failures with non-safety-critical processes or processing tasks do not adversely impact the ability of the processor interconnect or resources used for interfacing to support the integrity of SCF operations.
